newsitem.title: republic of ireland: FOCUS-Waterford, Avonmore in giant Irish food merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waterford, Avonmore in giant Irish food merger.

text.p: Ireland's Waterford Foods said on Tuesday it had agreed improved merger terms from Avonmore Foods Plc to create a dairy giant which would be one of the five biggest milk producers in the world.

Agreement was reached at a marathon meeting of the boards of Waterford Foods Plc and its associated farmers' co-operative in the southern town of Dungarvan overnight, and would be put to shareholders and co-op members for approval, a joint statement by Waterford and Avonmore said.
Avonmore's improved offer values the company at 337 million Irish pounds ($512 million) against an original offer of 281 million, the statement said.
If approved, it will weld together two of Ireland's premier food companies with a joint turnover of 2.5 billion pounds and pre-tax profits of 71.5 million.
This would create the largest dairy company in Britain and Ireland and the fourth largest milk processor in the world.
But some analysts said the planned merger could still fail due to a lack of support from farmers.
One food sector analyst, Liam Igoe of Goodbodys stockbrokers, said chances were only 50-50 that the merger would go ahead because farmers might not welcome the change.

"There's a lot of reluctance among some people to consider going down the merger route for whatever reason. It's to do with local loyalties and politics as much as the financial numbers and the commerciality of the deal," he told Reuters.

Analysts said the joint milk production of the two would far outstrip the dairy operations of Britain's Northern Foods Plc and Unigate Plc, and its cheese production would account for 20 percent of the British market.
To succeed the merger must be ratified by 75 percent of Waterford Co-op, which owns 68 percent of the Plc shares, and Waterford Foods Plc members.

"The boards of Avonmore and Waterford believe the proposed merger represents a unique opportunity to create a larger, more efficient and diversified Irish food group," the two companies said in a statement.
"The economies of scale achieved by combining both group's activities will create a stronger and more competitive base for their Irish operations," they said.

Under the proposal, Waterford Foods Plc shares will be valued at 142 pence compared with a closing price of 110 pence on the Dublin stock exchange on Monday night and 80 pence before Waterford said it had been approached by Avonmore last month.
Farmers trading with the new group will receive a "patronage bonus scheme" which would give milk producers supplying the group a premium of three pence per gallon for their produce.

Avonmore's previous offer in April was rejected by Waterford as inadequate. It is the second time in six years that Avonmore has attempted to merge with Waterford after a similar attempt in 1991 failed.
The two companies have considerable synergy which will allow for major economies of scale and cost-cutting, food industry analysts believe.
Waterford's profits and share price have plunged with margins squeezed by lower butter and milk prices, and the company issued a profit warning earlier this year.
But Avonmore has enjoyed a profitable year with a 13.7 percent rise in pre-tax profits to 36.45 million punts reported in March, bucking the trend in the Irish food sector.

The two companies have interests in Europe, Britain and America. Avonmore is Ireland's single biggest dairy company with interests in meat products, animal foodstuffs and agricultural products including grain.
It has processing operations in Ireland, Britain, Belgium and the United States, Japan, Korea and Singapore.
Waterford is engaged in dairy-based food products, fruit juices and animal foodstuffs and has processing plants in Ireland, Britain and America.
($ = 0.658 Irish Pounds)
